o1_0.name: Let's build a parking lot — without a class
o1_0.desc: Data separate, functions separate. Like most people write for the first time.
o1_0.what:
What does a parking lot need? A simple list:

• Some spots (places), each with size and floor
• Which car is parked on which spot
• A ticket when a car enters
• Calculate the money when exiting

Now write it in the simplest way: some arrays on top, some functions below. That's it.
o1_0.why:
This approach is not wrong. It is perfectly fine for small programs, and many good programs are written this way.

The problem starts when the program grows and multiple people work on it. And we will create that problem today — not from theory, but from our code.

How to do it:

Pay attention to one thing while writing: there is no relationship between data and the functions that modify it.

spots is an array. park() is a function. TypeScript does not know that they are related. Any other function can also modify spots — and no one will notice.

This may seem small now. By the end of the chapter it will become the biggest issue.
gotchas: Don't consider this code "bad". It works and is clear to read. The problem appears as it grows, not today.
Notice that spots, tickets, and earnings — all are declared at the top of the file. This is the entire subject of the next lesson.
terms: Code where data is separate and the functions that modify it are separate. There is no relationship between the two.
Data that resides at the top of the file and any function can modify it.
To change something (instead of creating a new one).

o0_0.name: Why TypeScript, and a 5-minute setup
o0_0.desc: TS = JavaScript + labels. And a way to run it without any heavy setup.
o0_0.what:
TypeScript is not a new language. It is JavaScript, where you can put a label on anything saying "this is a number", "this is a string", "this is a Vehicle".

These labels do not go to the browser. They are removed before execution and normal JavaScript remains. Their only purpose is to tell you about errors before the code runs.

Analogy: a label on a medicine bottle. The label is not part of the medicine — the patient doesn’t eat it. But because of the label you know before taking the wrong medicine.
o0_0.why:
This book gives TypeScript three features that plain JS does not have. You don’t need to understand them yet — just hear the names, each has its own chapter:

1. private and protected — with these you can say "this data can be accessed only from inside this class, not from outside". (Chapter 3)
2. interface — a list that describes what something can do, without saying how it does it. (Chapter 4)
3. abstract class — an incomplete class that must be completed before you can use it. (Chapter 4)

Learning OOP without these three is like learning cricket without a bat.

How to do it:

The simplest way to set up: tsx. It is a small tool that runs a TypeScript file directly — no compile step, no config.

npx tsx parking.ts — just that. The file will run.

But there is one issue: tsx only removes types, it does not check them. So errors will disappear silently. Therefore keep running npx tsc --noEmit --watch alongside — it sits in a separate terminal and continuously reports errors.

Two terminals: one to run, one to check. This is the complete book’s setup.
gotchas: "strict": true must be turned on. Without it TypeScript is half asleep and leaves many errors unchecked.
tsx does not check types, it only removes them. Therefore running a second terminal (tsc --watch) is necessary, otherwise you’ll think everything is fine.
The file extension must be .ts, not .js. It’s a small detail but can waste 10 minutes.
terms: JavaScript’s big brother — the same language, but you can put a label on everything saying "what type this is".
Transform TypeScript into regular JavaScript, because browsers only understand JavaScript.

o1_1.name: Now break this — and see who could have stopped it
o1_1.desc: Write four lines that make the entire system lie. And no one will even notice.
o1_1.what:
Now write four lines below. Everything will work. No error will occur. And all four will make your system lie.

It is important to understand: here TypeScript also cannot save you, because according to the types everything is correct. earnings is a number, and -99999 is also a number.
o1_1.why:
The real question is not "who will do it?". The real question is: if someone does it, how will we know?

In a 300 line file that three people are working on, anyone can touch spots at any time. And when a bug appears, you will have to search the entire file to find who changed what.

There is no way to find it — because the data is open to everyone.

How to do it:

Now write a rule that must always be true. Such a rule is called an invariant.

Our parking lot has three invariants:

1. earnings can never be negative.
2. A spot is either empty, or it has one car. Not two.
3. If a ticket is active, its spot must be occupied.

Today all three can be broken in your code, and the code won't even notice. This is the real output of this chapter.
gotchas: Don't think "I won't make that mistake". Six months later you will read this code yourself and won't remember which rule was what.
In a team this problem becomes ten times larger. A new person will change spots directly because they don't even know a rule existed.
TypeScript cannot save you here — according to the types everything is correct. This shows that types and design are two separate things.
terms: A rule that must always be true — e.g., "earnings can never be negative".
Data that is impossible — like a spot that is both empty and occupied.
o1_1.visualCap: Data lies open in the middle, and anyone can touch it directly. Every arrow is a point where a bug can slip in — and the system won't know who caused it.

o1_2.name: What is OOP — and what it promises
o1_2.desc: One-line answer: encapsulate the data and its rules in a container.
o1_2.what:
Definition: Object-Oriented Programming is a way of organizing code around objects — bundles that keep data and the operations on that data together, and control who is allowed to change what.

In simple terms: the data that should stay together and the rules that should apply to that data, put them in a container — and give the container a single entry point.

Analogy: ATM. Inside there is money, and it has rules (correct PIN, sufficient balance, not exceeding limit). You cannot open the machine and take money directly. You have to go through the door — insert card, enter PIN, request amount. At that door the machine checks every rule.

Procedural code is like breaking the ATM wall to take money. It works — but no rules are applied.
o1_2.why:
Now go back to the four breaking lines of Chapter 1. The single cure for all four is: do not let the data be touched directly.

If earnings can be changed only by one method (collectFee()), then:

• Writing earnings = -99999 becomes impossible
• And when earnings are wrong, you will have to look in one place only

This is OOP's first and biggest promise: "if something goes wrong, you will know where to look."

How to do it:

OOP has four major parts (people call them the "four pillars"). We will create all four, but not at once — as needed:

Encapsulation (Ch 3) — a door in front of the data. The direct answer to today’s problem.
Abstraction (Ch 4) — show only what the outside needs, hide the internal mess.
Inheritance (Ch 5) — a shared part for similar things in one place.
Polymorphism (Ch 6) — same name, different behavior for different things.

And an honest fact: OOP is not the answer to every problem. In Chapter 12 we will see when it is the wrong choice.
gotchas: OOP does not mean "create a class for everything". It can become a mountain of its own (Chapter 12 covers "God object" and over-engineering).
Don't try to cram all four pillars together. Each has its own chapter and will appear as the answer to a specific real problem.
terms: Object-Oriented Programming — organizing code around "things" (objects) where each thing has its own data and its own functions in one place.
An entity that has its own data and functions that operate on that data.
Encapsulating data in a container and putting a door in front of it — outsiders can only come through the door.
o1_2.visualCap: The same data, but now inside a container. Outsiders can only come through doors (methods), and each door checks the rules. Instead of a whole file being buggy — only the container.

o0_1.name: Type, interface, and union — describing the shape of data
o0_1.desc: You can describe how something looks inside in three ways.
o0_1.what:
Three things, all very simple:

1. Annotation — label with a colon: let age: number = 25.
2. Interface — a blueprint of an object: "it will have a plate that is a string, and a size that is a number".
3. Union — "one of these": type Size = "small" | "medium" | "large".

Union is the most useful. With it you can specify "only these three values are allowed", and if someone writes a fourth one they will get an error immediately.
o0_1.why:
These three will be immediately useful in a parking lot scenario. A vehicle's size can only be one of three values — small, medium, large. If it were a plain string, someone might write "smal" (typo) and that mistake would be discovered only at runtime, perhaps months later.

With a union, that mistake is caught instantly — and the editor will also suggest the three options.

How to do it:

You can create a blueprint of an object with both interface and type. There is not much difference. A simple rule for this book:

• Use interface when you are defining a blueprint that a class will implement (Chapter 4 will explain this fully).
• Use type for unions and for smaller shapes.

And a small note: ? means "this field is not required".
gotchas: Write Union options inside double quotes; without quotes they become variables: "small" is correct, small is wrong.
An optional field (?) can be undefined when read. You must check before using it, otherwise TypeScript will block it — and that is a good thing.
In 90% of cases, there is no difference between interface and type. Don't get stuck on this — the rule for this book is written above, just follow it.
terms: Label written with a colon — like let x: number.
A blueprint of an object — which fields it will have and their types.
"Either this or that" — like "car" | "bike", meaning one of the two.
A field marked with a question mark — it may be present or not.
o0_1.visualCap: Three tools, three purposes. Union is the most useful — it tells "only these values will work", and typos are caught instantly.

o0_2.name: Class syntax — field, constructor, method, this
o0_2.desc: Learn the syntax now. Its REAL meaning will be explained in Chapter 2.
o0_2.what:
Right now we are only looking at the syntax — why it matters will come in Chapter 2. For now just let your hand get used to it.

A class has four parts:

Field — data. plate: string;
Constructor — runs as soon as an object is created. Here fields get their initial value.
Method — work. Like a normal function, just don’t write the word function.
this — the "this object" inside a method.
o0_2.why:
Pause for a minute on this, because it causes the most confusion.

From a class you can create 1,000 objects. The method code is written only once, but it runs on 1,000 different objects. So inside a method you need the answer to “which object?” — that answer is this.

Analogy: In school there is a single form printed, and 500 students fill out that same form. The form says "write your name" — "your" means something different for each student. That is this.

How to do it:

TypeScript provides a shortcut that is very useful: if you write public/private directly on a constructor parameter, that field is created automatically.

In other words, three lines of work become one line. In this book we will use this shortcut everywhere — but first look at the longer way, so you know what the shortcut is doing.
gotchas: Forgetting to use this inside a method. If you write plate, TypeScript will say "Cannot find name plate" — because it’s a field, not a local variable.
Forgetting to use new. const v = Vehicle(...) is wrong, const v = new Vehicle(...) is correct.
this behaves differently inside an arrow function. Don’t get tangled in that now — in this book we will only use normal methods.
terms: A blueprint from which many similar things can be created.
Data stored inside a class — like a car’s number.
A function stored inside a class — like parking a car.
A special method that runs automatically when an object is created.
A real thing created from a class.
When written inside a method, it means "the object on which this method is running".

o2_0.desc: A blueprint, a thousand buildings. Each building has its own separate data.
o2_0.what:
Class is a blueprint. Object is the real thing created from that blueprint.

Analogy: a builder has a single flat blueprint. From that blueprint he builds 200 flats. The blueprint says "two rooms, one kitchen". But each flat has different people living, different belongings.

Blueprint = class. Flat = object. No one can live in the blueprint — you have to build a flat to live in it.

Therefore applying new is necessary. new ParkingLot() means "create a real parking lot from the blueprint".
o2_0.why:
This is not just a play on words. Its direct practical meaning is: each object has its own separate data.

If you need two parking lots — one for an airport, one for a mall — in procedural code you have to copy the entire file (because spots is a single global array). With a class you just write new twice.

This will be very useful up to Chapter 12, when we do testing: each test can create its own fresh parking lot, without being affected by the mess from previous tests.

How to do it:

Remember two words, because they are asked directly in interviews:

Class = definition, written once, exists as a single entity in memory.
Instance = an object created from that class, a new one each time you use new, with its own separate memory.

One more thing: methods are not copied for each object. The method code resides in one place; only the data differs. So even when you create 10,000 objects, the method code exists only once in memory.
gotchas: Forgetting to use new is the most common mistake. In TypeScript it will give an error; in plain JS it silently returns undefined.
Don't think of a class as an object. Writing class ParkingLot does not create a parking lot — it's just a blueprint. The real thing is created with new.
If you need a single instance throughout the program (like a single database connection), people use the Singleton pattern — but it is often the wrong choice. We'll see why in Chapter 11.
terms: A blueprint — describes what the thing will have, but it is not the thing itself.
A real thing created from a blueprint. You can create as many as you want from a class.
The keyword that creates a new real thing from a blueprint.
o2_0.visualCap: A blueprint, three real things. The blueprint only specifies "what it will be"; the actual data belongs to each object. The method code resides in one place — only the data differs.

o2_1.name: Make the parking lot a class — data and behavior in one place
o2_1.desc: Same code, but now spots and park() are parts of the same thing.
o2_1.what:
Now we put the same procedural code into a class. Behavior will not change at all — only the location will change.

The global spots becomes this.spots. The global park() becomes a method. And now both are parts of the same thing.

Improving the structure without changing behavior is called refactor. We will do this repeatedly in this book.
o2_1.why:
Two things improve immediately:

1. Readability. Now anyone opening the ParkingLot class will see in one place what data it holds and what operations are performed on it. Previously they had to scan the entire file.

2. Counting. Now you can count how many places spots is modified from — because it is only inside the class. (It can still be accessed from outside, but now you know where to look.)

This is called cohesion: things that should stay together do stay together. This will become a full topic in Chapter 9.

How to do it:

When refactoring follow one rule: one thing at a time.

First move only the data inside and run the code. Then move one method at a time, running each time. If you change everything at once, you won’t know what broke when something fails.

And a small but very useful point: Should ParkingLot, Spot, and Ticket each be separate classes? Answer: yes, if they have their own rules. Spot has its own rules (empty/occupied), Ticket also has (when it entered, how long it stayed). So all three classes will be created.
gotchas: Don’t refactor everything at once. First move the data inside and run it. Then move one method and run it. This discipline will save you in larger refactors later.
Don’t forget to add this. — if you write spots.find(...) you’ll get an error because it is now a field, not a global. This is a good error; it shows that the refactor actually happened.
You might want to keep Spot and Ticket as just interfaces (plain objects). But they have their own rules (isFree, hoursParked), so they should be classes — data together with its behavior.
terms: Things that should stay together do stay together. High cohesion = good design.
Improving the structure of code without changing its behavior.

o2_2.name: Constructor — create object in correct state
o2_2.desc: An object must be valid as soon as it is created. Half-built objects are the biggest bugs.
o2_2.what:
Constructor is a special method that runs automatically when you use new. Its sole purpose is to bring the object into a correct state as soon as it is created.

If you don’t write a constructor, TypeScript assumes an empty constructor — and your object is created without any data.
o2_2.why:
This may sound minor, but it is very important: an object should never exist in an incorrect state — not even for a moment.

Imagine a ParkingLot whose name is empty and spots is undefined. That is a “half-built” object. If someone calls park() on it, it will crash — and from the crash you will never know that the real mistake happened while creating the object.

Therefore the rule: perform validation inside the constructor and never allow an object to be created with invalid data.

How to do it:

In TypeScript, constructor overloading is not real — you cannot write two separate constructors. There are three approaches:

1. Optional parameters — constructor(name: string, floors = 1)
2. A single object parameter — constructor(config: LotConfig). When there are more than 3 parameters, this is the best choice.
3. Static factory method — ParkingLot.fromConfig(...). You can give it a name, which you cannot do with a constructor.

The third approach becomes the Factory pattern in Chapter 11. For now just note that it originates here.
gotchas: Don’t perform heavy work (database calls, file reads, network requests) inside a constructor. Object creation should be instantaneous. Use a static factory for heavy operations.
Don’t return anything from a constructor. It automatically returns the object; an explicit return leads to unexpected behavior.
If you end up with more than 3 parameters, switch to an object parameter. After 6 months, no one will be able to tell what each argument in new Lot("A", 5, 100, 0, true) represents.
terms: A special method that runs automatically when an object is created — it sets the object's initial state.
A condition where all of the object's invariants hold true.
Multiple versions of the same name for different argument lists. In JavaScript/TypeScript this isn’t actually supported.

o3_2.name: Invariants — put the rule at the door
o3_2.desc: Now that the path is single, the check will be in one place. And then it will never break.
o3_2.what:
In Chapter 1 you wrote three invariants:

1. earnings is never negative
2. At most one car per spot
3. A spot with a live ticket must be occupied

Now that the data is private and the path to change is one, the check can also be placed in one place — and then that rule will never break.
o3_2.why:
This is the real reward of encapsulation, and it is far bigger than "hiding".

In procedural code, if you want earnings to never be negative, you have to place a check at every location where earnings change — and forgetting one place was enough.

Now? There is a single location. A single check. And that check cannot be bypassed, because there is no alternative path.

How to do it:

There are two ways to handle invalid input:

1. throw — "this should never happen, it’s a programmer error". Like a negative fee.
2. return null or a result object — "this can happen, it’s normal". Like a full parking.

The difference is: throw for things that are bugs, return for things that are part of normal operation. A full parking is not a bug; it happens regularly. A negative fee is a bug.

And fail fast: stop as soon as an error occurs. Don’t silently 0 return and continue — that hides the bug and causes a crash elsewhere later.
gotchas: Don’t throw for everything. "Parking full" happens regularly — it should return null, not an error. Otherwise the caller has to wrap every call in try/catch.
Silently returning 0 or null to hide a bug is the most dangerous. In the Chapter 1 code, unpark() returned 0 for an invalid ticket — and that bug was never caught.
Place the rule in the class that owns it. "One spot, one car" is not a ParkingLot rule — it’s a Spot rule. This way ParkingLot cannot violate it.
terms: A rule that must always be true.
A check placed at the start of a method that prevents invalid input from entering.
Stop immediately when an error occurs, instead of proceeding and silently doing the wrong thing.

o3_3.name: Your Error classes — turn mistakes into objects
o3_3.desc: throw new Error("something went wrong") prevents the caller from doing anything. Error should also be a class.
o3_3.what:
Currently your code writes like this:

throw new Error("Spot is full")

This works. But consider what the caller receives — just a string. And code cannot make decisions based on a string.

If the UI needs to know that "parking is full, show a different message; but if the plate is wrong, highlight the form" — it would have to write e.message === "Spot is full". And the day you change a single word in the message, its code will silently break.
o3_3.why:
The solution is exactly what's in the book: turn mistakes into objects (class).

Then you get three benefits:

1. The caller can recognize them with instanceof — and this is one of the 10% places where instanceof is correct (Chapter 6).
2. An Error can carry data — which spot, which plate, how long.
3. By creating a common parent, the caller can catch the whole family in a single catch.

How to do it:

A small but important TypeScript detail: when you write class MyError extends Error, instanceof sometimes does not work (on older compile targets). The fix is one line — in the constructor call Object.setPrototypeOf(this, new.target.prototype).

And a design rule: do not create a separate Error class for every tiny case. A common parent (ParkingError) and its 3-4 children are enough. If the caller does not differentiate between two errors, there is no reason to separate them.
gotchas: After extending Error, you must call Object.setPrototypeOf(this, new.target.prototype); otherwise instanceof may sometimes return false — and this bug is very hard to find.
Do not create a separate Error class for every tiny thing. If the caller does not differentiate between two errors, there is no reason to separate them.
In catch (e), don’t forget to write "else throw e". Swallowing an error that isn’t yours is the most dangerous — that bug hides forever.
Don’t throw errors for normal situations (like parking full). It’s still a return null case — the Chapter 3 rule applies here as well.
terms: A thing that occurs when something goes wrong, and that stops the code and propagates upward.
Throwing an error — "I cannot proceed further".
Exception hierarchy — a family of your Error classes where all share a common parent.

o4_1.name: Interface — "I can do this" promise
o4_1.desc: Only name and shape. No code. And a class can take multiple interfaces.
o4_1.what:
A interface is just a list: "any class that takes this interface must have these methods."

It contains no code — only names, arguments, and return types. It is a promise, not an implementation.

Analogy: an electrical socket. The socket says "two pins, this distance apart". Now you can plug in a fan, a charger, or a lamp — the socket doesn't care. Socket = interface, plug = class that implements it.
o4_1.why:
The real benefit of an interface is: a class can take multiple interfaces.

A car can be Parkable and also Chargeable (if it's electric). A payment method can be PaymentMethod and also Refundable.

This doesn't happen with classes — a class can have only one parent (we'll see why in Chapter 5). So when something can be of many kinds, an interface is the right answer.

How to do it:

In TypeScript there is a small but important point: writing implements is not mandatory.

TypeScript uses "structural typing" — meaning if your class has the correct methods, it will automatically work as that interface, whether or not you wrote implements.

Still, write implements. Because it provides two things: (1) the reader instantly knows the intention, and (2) if you mistakenly misspell a method name, the error will appear in the class, not ten files away where it is used.
gotchas: An interface exists only at compile time — it disappears at runtime. Therefore you cannot write "x instanceof PaymentMethod". You need to keep a field (e.g., name) for that.
Writing implements is optional but you should write it. Otherwise, if you misspell a method name, the error will appear ten files away, making it hard to locate.
Do not put too many methods in an interface. If a class has to leave half the methods empty, the interface should be split — this is Chapter 10's "I" (Interface Segregation).
terms: A list that only specifies which operations are possible — not their code.
A class stating that "I fulfill the promise of this interface".
Promise — if you write implements, you must implement every method.

o3_0.name: public, private, protected — who can see what
o3_0.desc: Three levels. And a fourth thing that is different in TypeScript and JavaScript.
o3_0.what:
There are three levels, and all three answer the same question: "who can touch this?"

public — anyone. This is the default, so if you don’t specify anything, everything is public.
private — only code written inside that class.
protected — code of that class, and code of its children (subclasses). (Children will appear in Chapter 5.)
o3_0.why:
This is not just for "hiding". Its real benefit is: when you make something private, you can later change that thing without affecting anyone.

Imagine you turned #spots from an array into a Map because you wanted faster lookups. If it were public, every place in the codebase that wrote lot.spots[0] would break. Since it’s private, only the code inside the class needs to change.

This is called "the freedom to change" — and it’s the most valuable thing in large codebases.

How to do it:

In TypeScript, private can be written in two ways, and there’s a big difference between them:

1. private balance — TypeScript’s private. It is checked only at compile time. At runtime it is a normal field; anyone can write (lot as any).balance to access it.

2. #balance — JavaScript’s true private. It remains private at runtime. Trying to access it from outside throws a real error.

In this book we will use # where the data truly needs to be protected, and private where we only want to indicate "this is internal". This distinction is asked about in interviews.
gotchas: Don’t make everything private. Anything that external code needs should be public — otherwise people will look for workarounds and the design will suffer.
For a # field, the "target" in tsconfig must be ES2022 or newer. With an older target, TypeScript generates a weird WeakMap-based code that is slow.
readonly only prevents reassignment. In a readonly spots: Spot[] you can still do spots.push(). Many people forget this — Chapter 9 covers it fully.
terms: Anyone can see it, anyone can change it. This is the default.
Only code inside that class can see it.
Inside that class, and inside its children (subclasses). It will be useful in Chapter 5.
These three words — they indicate who can touch what.

o4_2.name: Abstract class — an incomplete class that must be completed
o4_2.desc: Provides some code, and requires you to write some. And it is sometimes better than an interface.
o4_2.what:
Abstract class is a class that is incomplete. You cannot instantiate it directly — you must first complete it.

It contains two kinds of things:

• Concrete methods — same for everyone, with code.
• Abstract methods — only a name, no code. Each subclass must implement them.

Analogy: a half-filled form. Some fields are pre-filled (school name, address) — same for everyone. Some are empty (your name, roll number) — each student must fill them. The half-filled form itself is not a student; it needs to be completed.
o4_2.why:
The only major difference between an interface and an abstract class is:

Interface — only a promise, no code. A class can implement many.
Abstract class — promise and shared code. A class can extend only one.

Therefore the rule is simple:

• If you have shared code that is the same for all subclasses → abstract class
• If there is only a promise and each will provide its own implementation → interface
• If something can have multiple forms → interface (because a class can have only one parent)

How to do it:

In our parking lot: every vehicle has a plate, and describe() can be the same for all. But getSize() and getHourlyRate() are specific to each vehicle.

So: some shared, some different — exactly the abstract-class situation.

And a very useful fact: you can use both together. An abstract class that implements an interface — this is the most common pattern in real code.
gotchas: An abstract class can have a constructor — and it should, because shared data is set there. You just can't instantiate it directly.
If an abstract class has no abstract methods, it probably doesn't need to be abstract.
Abstract classes invite deep hierarchies (Vehicle → Car → ElectricCar → ...). This will become a Chapter 7 wall. Enjoy now, the pain later.
In TypeScript, an abstract class behaves like a normal class at runtime. "abstract" is only a compiler label.
terms: An incomplete class — you cannot instantiate it directly, you must complete it.
Only a name, no code — the subclass must implement it.
A fully built class that can be instantiated.

o4_3.name: ADT — difference between interface and implementation
o4_3.desc: Stack, Queue, Map — these are "what it does", not "how it is built".
o4_3.what:
This is the clearest example of abstraction, and it is asked a lot in interviews.

Stack what is it? It is a thing where you can push and pop, and the last thing you put in comes out first.

Note — I did not explain what it is internally. It can be built from an array, a linked list, or something else. A Stack is an ADT: it is identified by its behavior, not by its structure.
o4_3.why:
This teaches a big point: List, Stack, Queue, Map, Set — all of these are interfaces. And ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap, TreeMap — these are implementations.

And because of this, a very useful rule emerges: "program to an interface, not an implementation."

In other words, write in your code "I need a List", not "I need an ArrayList". Then you can change the implementation later and nobody's code will break.

How to do it:

We have a direct use for this in our parking lot. Right now #spots is an array. Tomorrow it could become a Map (for faster lookup), or a database (when the lot grows).

If we create a SpotRepository interface — "you can find spots, you can save them" — then ParkingLot will never know whether the underlying storage is an array or a database.

This is the seed of Chapter 10’s "D" (Dependency Inversion). Just keep in mind that it comes from here.
gotchas: Don't create a repository interface for every tiny thing. That's over-engineering. Create an interface only when you truly need more than two implementations or a mock for testing.
In JavaScript, an Array is essentially used as a List, Stack, and Queue all together (push/pop/shift). Therefore this distinction isn't visible in JS — but it is asked in interviews.
Don't name the interface "IParkingLot". That's an old C# convention. Keep the name clean: SpotRepository, PaymentMethod.
terms: Abstract Data Type — a data structure's definition based on its behavior, not its internal structure.
Implementation — a way to actually build that ADT — using an array, a linked list, or something else.

o4_4.name: Generics — a framework, many types
o4_4.desc: A single Repository that works for Spot and also for Ticket — without losing the type.
o4_4.what:
You created SpotRepository. Tomorrow you will need TicketRepository, then VehicleRepository. The code for all three will be exactly the same — only the type differs.

There are two bad approaches:

1. Copy-paste — three files, identical code. Bugs also have to be fixed in three places.
2. Use any — a single Repository that stores “anything”. But then the result of repo.find() will also be any, and you lose all the benefits of TypeScript.

Generics is the third solution: leave a placeholder for the type, and fill it in when you use it.
o4_4.why:
This is just a form of abstraction — one level higher.

An interface says: "I need this functionality, any implementation is fine."
A generic says: "I need this structure, any type is fine."

And most importantly: unlike any, a generic does not lose the type. Repository<Spot>'s find() gives you a Spot, not any. So you get convenience and safety.

You are already using this, perhaps without noticing: Array<number>, Map<string, Spot>, Set<string> — all three are generics.

How to do it:

The most useful thing is a constraint — applying extends to set a condition on the placeholder.

class Repository<T> — T can be anything. But then you cannot write item.id, because T might have an id or might not.

class Repository<T extends { id: string }> — now T can be anything that has an id. And writing item.id is safe.

A warning: create a generic only when you truly need it for more than one type. Making a generic for a single type only makes the code harder to read.
gotchas: Do not create a generic for a single type. If you only need Spot, a plain SpotRepository is better — generics add overhead to readability.

o5_2.name: The single-parent rule — and Diamond Problem
o5_2.desc: Why multiple parents aren't allowed, and how an interface fixes it.
o5_2.what:
In TypeScript (and Java, C#) a class can have only one parent. Writing class A extends B, C is not allowed.

Why? Because there is a deep issue called the diamond problem.

Imagine: Vehicle has a describe(). ElectricVehicle and CommercialVehicle both inherit from Vehicle and both have overridden describe() in their own way. Now ElectricTruck inherits from both — which describe() will run?

There is no clear answer. Therefore most languages say: "we will not allow this problem to occur."
o5_2.why:
This is where the real benefit of interfaces becomes clear.

An interface contains no code — only a contract. So if two interfaces have the same method name, there is no conflict: both are simply saying "this method should exist", and your class implements it once.

Therefore the rule becomes: "one parent for code. As many interfaces as you want for contracts."

How to apply:

Practical decision:

• extends — one. Where there is shared code.
• implements — as many as you need. Where you only need to specify the shape.

And if you really need code from two places? That is a sign that inheritance is the wrong tool — you need composition. That is Chapter 8.

TypeScript also has a trick called a mixin that works like multiple inheritance. It works, but the code is heavy to read. In this book we will choose composition.
gotchas: In TypeScript, mixins can achieve something like multiple inheritance, but the resulting code is heavy to read. You can mention it in an interview, but choose composition by default.
If two interfaces have a method with the same name but different signatures, TypeScript will give an error. If the signatures are the same, there is no problem.
"I need code from two places" — this is always a signal that something is wrong in the design. Pause and consider whether those things are truly "is-a" relationships.
terms: A class can have only one parent.
Multiple parents — not allowed for classes in TypeScript/Java.

o5_0.name: extends and super — free stuff
o5_0.desc: A child receives everything from the parent, and can add its own.
o5_0.what:
class Car extends Vehicle means: "Car has everything that Vehicle has, plus its own."

A child receives all of the parent’s public and protected fields/methods. private (#) is not received — it belongs only to the parent.

super is used in two places:

• super(...) in a constructor — “run the parent’s constructor first”.
• super.method() — “run the parent’s version”.
o5_0.why:
The benefit is straightforward: shared code in one place. If every vehicle needs ownerName, you write it once in Vehicle and all three children get it.

Another big benefit: a Car can be used wherever a Vehicle is expected. Therefore ParkingLot.park(vehicle: Vehicle) can accept Car, Bike, Truck — all of them, without knowing the specific type.

This is called an "is-a" relationship: Car is a kind of Vehicle. Remember this test, because in Chapter 7 we will use this test to determine when inheritance is inappropriate.

How to do it:

Two rules that TypeScript enforces:

1. In the child’s constructor, super(...) must appear first — before using this. Because until the parent part is constructed, the object is incomplete.
2. Any abstract method defined in the parent must be implemented by the child.

And a rule that TypeScript does not enforce but you should follow: use inheritance only for “is-a” relationships. Not for “has-a” relationships. This distinction is the entire topic of Chapter 8.

# private members are not inherited by children. If a child needs it, use protected — but consider whether it’s truly needed.
If you forget to write super.method() and just call method(), it will invoke itself — causing an infinite loop and stack overflow. This is a classic bug.
Don’t give a child a field the same name as a parent field. It hides the parent’s field (shadowing) and makes bugs impossible to track.

o5_1.name: Method overriding — the parent’s work in your own way
o5_1.desc: Same name, different behavior. And a rule that, when broken, messes everything up.
o5_1.what:
Overriding means: the method in the parent, the child rewrites it in its own way. The name and signature stay the same, but the behavior changes.

And when you call vehicle.describe(), the object’s version runs — even if the variable’s type is Vehicle.
o5_1.why:
Now a very important rule. When overriding, the child must not break the parent’s contract.

That means: if someone writes code expecting a Vehicle, giving it a Truck should not cause the code to break.

This is called the Liskov Substitution Principle (referred to as "L" in Chapter 10). Remember this line: "the child should silently work in place of the parent."

How to do it:

Three things that are incorrect when overriding:

1. Adding new conditions. The parent accepted any license plate, the child says "only plates from MH will work" → code that assumed Vehicle will break.
2. Reducing guarantees. The parent said "always provide a number", the child sometimes returns null → caller crashes.
3. Throwing an exception where the parent did not.

In TypeScript you can write the override keyword (you can also make it required by turning noImplicitOverride on in tsconfig). It prevents a mistake: if the method does not exist in the parent (e.g., you misspelled the name), you get an error.
gotchas: noImplicitOverride: true must be turned on. If the method name has a typo, it silently creates a new method and the old one keeps running — the hardest-to-find bug.
After overriding, just calling super.method() and doing nothing else — that’s useless code, remove it.
Don’t call an overridden method from a constructor. At that point the child’s constructor hasn’t run yet, so the child’s fields will be undefined. This is a classic Java/C# trap.
terms: Rewrite the parent’s method in the child, in your own way.
Method name + its arguments + return type.
The child can be used in place of the parent without breaking anything. (Full description in Chapter 10)

o6_1.desc: The names are similar, but the work is completely different. It is definitely asked in interviews.
o6_1.what:
These two terms appear in every OOP interview, and people mix them up. The difference is straightforward:

Overriding — in different classes, with the same signature. "A child does the parent’s work in its own way." Which one works is determined at runtime.

Overloading — within the same class, with a different signature. "Same name, different version for different arguments." Which one works is known at compile time.
o6_1.why:
And an important point: Overloading is not real in JavaScript.

JavaScript can have only one function with a given name. TypeScript lets you write "overload signatures", but they are only labels — in reality a single function is created that you have to handle yourself with if.

In Java/C# overloading is real — there you actually get separate methods.

How to remember:

The easiest way to remember:

Overriding — id = identity. A new entity (class) does the same work.
Overloading — load = burden. The same entity lifts a different burden (arguments).

And a practical tip: avoid overloading in TypeScript. Use optional parameters or union types instead — the code stays clean and stays in one place.
gotchas: With TypeScript overload signatures, the implementation signature is not visible from the outside. If you forget, the caller will see only a single version.
Do not treat overloading as the "real" form of polymorphism. Real polymorphism is overriding — it works at runtime and automatically adapts to new types.
If interviewers ask about "compile-time vs runtime polymorphism", these are the two points: overloading = compile-time, overriding = runtime.
terms: Rewriting the parent’s method in the child. Decided at runtime.
Multiple methods with the same name, different arguments. Decided at compile time.
Another name for overriding — the object decides at runtime.
Another name for overloading — the compiler decides at compile time.

o6_2.name: Apply across the whole system — and measure
o6_2.desc: Find every if-else chain, remove it, and count the difference.
o6_2.what:
Now apply this thinking across the entire parking lot. Find three kinds of smell in your code:

1. a check using instanceof or constructor.name
2. switch (type) or if (type === "...")
3. a property whose name is "type" or "kind" and has branching on it

Replace each with a single method call.
o6_2.why:
When a small change requires opening five files, it’s called shotgun surgery — and it’s the most expensive problem because there’s a chance of forgetting a place each time.

Polymorphism is its direct cure: a new type = a new file, everything else stays the same.

And this can be measured — that’s the milestone of this chapter.

How to do it:

A small but powerful pattern: if you want a "default" behavior along with polymorphism, create a normal method in the parent (not abstract), and let subclasses override it as needed.

And one place where instanceof is appropriate: when an object comes from outside (JSON, library) and you have no control over it. First convert it to your type, then use polymorphism.
gotchas: Don’t make everything polymorphic. If a behavior is only for one class and never needed by another, there’s no need to put it in the parent.
If the parent ends up with 15 abstract methods, every new subclass will have to implement 15 methods. That’s a sign that the hierarchy is doing too much — it will be named in Chapter 7.
Providing a default behavior doesn’t mean it’s always safe. If the default is wrong, a new subclass will silently behave incorrectly. Consider: should it be default or abstract?

o7_1.name: Fragile base class — one line in the parent, children break
o7_1.desc: Inheritance is a very strong bond. And a strong bond hurts more when it breaks.
o7_1.what:
One aspect of inheritance that people mention less: children know the code inside their parent and depend on it.

If the parent changes its internal implementation — even if its external behavior stays exactly the same — the children can break.

This is called white-box reuse: you have to open the internal box to see it in order to reuse. The opposite is black-box reuse — just use the external interface, the internal details don't matter. (That will appear in Chapter 8.)
o7_1.why:
A classic example, and it's real:

The parent has park() which internally calls parkOne(). The child overrides parkOne() to increment a counter.

Now the parent’s developer optimizes park() — it no longer calls parkOne(), it does the work directly. The parent’s external behavior is exactly the same. But the child’s counter silently stops working.

And the worst part: the parent’s developer doesn’t even know that something broke.

How to handle it:

Therefore a big rule: design a class either for inheritance (and document which method is called when), or seal it.

In Java final, in C# sealed. TypeScript has no such keyword — but you can achieve the same with a private constructor or composition.

And a practical tip: have a method in your own class call another method — don’t let children depend on that. If it is necessary, document it (this is called "self-use documentation").
gotchas: This problem is the biggest for library authors. If external code extends your class, you can never change your internal code.
A protected method is part of the public API — even if it is declared "protected". As soon as someone overrides it, you cannot break it.
It doesn’t appear until something breaks. And when it breaks, the bug shows up in a completely unexpected place (the counter is zero) rather than where the actual change occurred.
terms: A parent class where even a small change breaks its children.
Two things are so tightly linked that when one changes, the other breaks.
Reuse where you need to know the internal code — inheritance works that way.

o6_0.name: Don't ask who you are — just give the task
o6_0.desc: Replace the instanceof chain with a single method call.
o6_0.what:
There are two ways to get the work done:

Method 1 (bad) — ask around: "Are you a Car? Then 30. Are you a Bike? Then 20."
Method 2 (good) — state the task: "What is your rate?" And each vehicle answers itself.

In the second approach, your code doesn't even know which vehicle it is dealing with. This is called dynamic dispatch — at runtime the object itself decides which version will run.

Analogy: managers come in two types. One asks every person "Are you a designer? Then do this. Are you a developer? Then do that." The other simply says "Do your job" — and each person knows what their job is. The second manager scales, the first does not.
o6_0.why:
if-else chain has three problems:

1. Adding a new type means you have to edit the existing file. And you have to do it in every place where that chain appears.
2. It's very easy to forget a place. And the compiler won't warn you.
3. The chain gets scattered. One chain in pricing, another in a report, another in an allotment — you have to update all three.

With polymorphism: a new type = a new class, and the compiler will only accept you after you implement each method.

How to do it:

The refactoring approach is straightforward, three steps:

1. Locate the if-else/switch chain that is based on the type.
2. Turn each branch of that chain into a method inside the corresponding class.
3. Replace the chain with a single method call.

And an important signal: if you are writing instanceof, there is a 90% chance that polymorphism should be used there. (In about 10% of cases it is truly necessary — such as checking error types.)

"default" or "else" branches are the most dangerous — they silently give wrong answers for new types. In polymorphism there is no default.
Don't make everything abstract in Vehicle. If something applies only to a single subclass (e.g., Truck's needsPermit), keep it in that subclass only.

o7_2.name: is-a test fail — when "a kind of" becomes a lie
o7_2.desc: Remember the Chapter 5 test? Today it will fail — and that's the real signal.
o7_2.what:
In Chapter 5 we said: use inheritance when "is-a" is true. Today we see that question isn’t that easy.

Classic example: Is a Square a kind of Rectangle?

In mathematics — yes. In code — no. Because Rectangle promises that "width and height can be set independently", and Square breaks that promise.
o7_2.why:
And the same thing is happening in our parking lot. Consider:

Is a Motorcycle a kind of Bike? Yes in shape. But if the Bike promises "can park without a permit" and a motorcycle needs a permit — that promise is broken.

Is a ElectricCar a kind of Car? Yes... but if you changed maxHours() from 24 to 8, the code that assumed a Car could make a 12-hour booking will break.

In other words is-a is not just a shape question, it’s a behavior question. This is called behavioural subtyping.

How to do it:

The real test is (and this is the Chapter 5 contract test):

"Can I replace the parent with the child everywhere and nothing breaks?"

If the answer is "yes, but..." then is-a has failed. Anything that comes after "but" is a bug.

And when is-a fails, inheritance is the wrong tool. Use has-a instead: instead of creating a parent, make a field. That’s Chapter 8.
gotchas: A contract test failing isn’t bad — it’s telling you there’s a design mistake. Fixing the test to make it pass and hiding the failure is the biggest deception.
Don’t write an is-a test based only on the name. "ElectricCar is a Car" sounds true by name. Test the behavior, not the name.
If the child has many overrides that change the parent’s behavior, it might not be a child at all. Count them: 2-3 overrides are fine, more than 6 is a signal.
terms: "Is X a kind of Y?" — the question that tells whether inheritance is appropriate.
The child can replace the parent without breaking anything.
Having only the shape isn’t enough — the behavior must also match.

o8_0.name: has-a — make the thing a field
o8_0.desc: One line change, and 24 classes become 4.
o8_0.what:
Inheritance says: "Car is a kind of Vehicle." (is-a)
Composition says: "Car has an Engine as." (has-a)

Now look at "being electric". It is not a type — it is a property. So instead of creating a class, make a thing:

class Car { #power: PowerSource }

And PowerSource can be either Battery or PetrolTank.
o8_0.why:
Now see how all three walls of Chapter 7 fall:

1. Explosion ends. 3 independent things = 3 fields, not 8 classes. Vehicle types remain 3.

2. Fragile base class eliminated. Car does not know the code inside Battery — it only calls battery.charge(). Battery can change its internals whenever it wants, and Car will not break. This is black-box reuse.

3. The is-a question disappears. Now there is no "a kind of", so the promise of inheritance breaking does not arise.

And a bonus that inheritance cannot do at all: a field can be changed while running. Turn a petrol car into an electric one — in one line.

How to do it:

Refactoring steps:

1. Look at each subclass and ask: "what does it add?" (battery, permit, valet)
2. Create a small class for that thing.
3. Add a field for it in the parent class.
4. Delete the subclass.

And a good habit: make those things interfaces (PowerSource) instead of concrete classes. Then new types can be added without affecting anyone.
gotchas: Don't create a class for every tiny thing. If the thing is just a boolean and has no behavior, keep it as a boolean. Create a class only when it has its own responsibilities.
Providing default values is necessary, otherwise you'll have to write new Car("A","x", new PetrolTank(40), new StandardAccess(), new RegularService()) everywhere — and that's hard to read.
If there are more than four items, switch to a constructor object parameter (the lesson from Chapter 2).
Composition does not mean abandoning inheritance entirely. Vehicle -> Car is still inheritance, and that's correct because a Car really is a kind of Vehicle.
terms: Keeping other objects inside an object and having them do the work.
"It HAS that thing" — Car has a Battery.
Having the inner object do the work instead of doing it yourself.
Using only the external interface without knowing the internal code.

o8_1.name: Delegation — pass the work forward
o8_1.desc: Make the inner object do the work. And decide "how far to pass it forward".
o8_1.what:
When you call car.getHourlyRate() and inside it calls this.service.rateMultiplier() — that is called delegation. The car is not doing the work itself; it is having the inner object do it.

This is the second half of composition. Making something a field is the first half; having it do the work is the second.
o8_1.why:
The big benefit of delegation is that the Car decides what is exposed externally.

In inheritance, the parent’s entire public API automatically appears in the child — whether you want it or not. In composition you choose what to pass forward.

Therefore, with composition your public API stays small and deliberately designed. With inheritance it keeps expanding on its own.

How to do it:

A real problem: if the inner object has 10 methods needed externally, you have to write 10 one-line methods. That is called boilerplate, and it is the real cost of composition.

Three approaches:

1. Write only the methods that are actually needed externally (often 3 out of 10).
2. Expose the inner object with a readonly getter — but encapsulation is reduced a bit.
3. Create an interface that both implement.

In most cases the first is correct — and that boilerplate is actually a benefit, because it forces you to think about what is needed externally.
gotchas: Exposing the inner object via a getter (get battery() { return this.#battery; }) — this breaks encapsulation and external code starts working directly on it.
Don’t put logic in delegation methods. It’s fine if a method only forwards; if it does a 10-line job, the logic probably belongs elsewhere.
Having to write many delegation methods is a signal that the functionality maybe shouldn’t be inside, or your class is doing too much (the God object from Chapter 12).
terms: Having the inner object do the work instead of doing it yourself.
A class that hides inner objects and provides a clean entry point.

o8_2.desc: Both have their own responsibilities. A decision list you can remember.
o8_2.what:
This chapter is not saying "inheritance is bad". Inheritance is absolutely correct when used in the right place.

In your code, Car extends Vehicle is still there — and that's correct, because Car is truly a type of Vehicle, and it doesn't break any promise.

The part that should be removed is ElectricCar extends Car — because "being electric" was a feature, not a type.
o8_2.why:
Industry advice is: "favor composition over inheritance" — meaning choose composition when in doubt. Statistics show that people misuse inheritance many times more than they misuse composition.

But "favor" does not mean "never use it". Inheritance has three proper uses:

1. Shared code + is-a when it truly holds (Vehicle → Car)
2. Framework contract when a library says "extend my class"
3. Abstract class when you need to provide some code and require some implementation

How to do it:

A decision list. Ask these four questions for every new relationship:

1. Can I replace the parent with a child everywhere, without any "but"?
2. Is this a type or a feature? (Feature = composition)
3. Can this change at runtime? (Yes = composition, because the class does not change)
4. Can this combine with multiple things? (Yes = composition, otherwise explosion)

If composition is the answer in even one place, choose composition.
gotchas: Inheritance should not be completely abandoned. Vehicle → Car is still correct, and abstract classes are very useful.
Don't memorize "favor composition". Remember the four questions — they will work for every new case, whether it's a parking lot or anything else.
Composition increases the number of objects. That's fine — small, single-purpose classes are far better than a large hierarchy.
terms: A well-known recommendation: choose composition when in doubt.
Provide behavior as an object from the outside — which you just created today without naming it.
o8_2.visualCap: Four questions, one decision. If composition is the answer anywhere, choose composition — because fixing misuse of inheritance is very expensive.

o8_3.name: Three forms of has-a — Composition, Aggregation, Association
o8_3.desc: Not all "has-a" are alike. The question is: who is the owner, and who dies with whom.
o8_3.what:
Until now we considered "has-a" as a single thing. But in reality it has three forms, and the difference is revealed by a single question:

"If the outer thing disappears, what will happen to the inner thing?"

Composition — the inner thing also disappears. The ParkingLots of a Spot: if the lot no longer exists, the spots have no meaning. Spots are created inside the lot.

Aggregation — the inner thing stays alive. The ParkingLot of a PricingPolicy: the lot is closed, but the same pricing can be used by another lot. It was created outside and was injected.

Association — there is no owner. Ticket and Vehicle: both know each other, but neither creates nor destroys the other.
o8_3.why:
This is not just a naming game — it tells where the object will be created.

Composition → create with new inside. this.#spots.push(new Spot(...)). This is one place where writing new is correct (an exception to Chapter 9’s “don’t write new in the domain” rule).

Aggregation → obtain from the constructor. This is Dependency Injection (Chapter 9). In other words, you used DI because the relationship was aggregation, not composition.

Association → keep only a reference, or just its id.

And interviewers often ask directly “what is the difference between composition and aggregation” — the answer is always lifecycle and ownership.

How to do it:

A small but very useful decision: in an association you don’t need to keep the whole object — often just the id is better.

If you keep the entire Ticket inside a Vehicle, the ticket will keep that vehicle alive (in memory), and when you save the ticket you’ll also have to save the whole vehicle. Keep only the plate — it works and the relationship stays loose.

And an honest point: in everyday conversation people call all three "composition" (as in “composition over inheritance”). That isn’t wrong — just know that UML defines three distinct concepts so you can explain the difference in an interview.
gotchas: In composition, writing new inside is correct — it’s an exception to Chapter 9’s “don’t write new in the domain” rule. That rule was for AGGREGATION (which should come from outside).
In composition, don’t expose the inner array directly. Return a copy ([...arr]) or a readonly version in the getter, otherwise the external code becomes the owner and the relationship breaks.
Think before keeping the whole object in an association. Often just the id is enough, and it makes both memory usage and save/load easier.
In everyday talk people call all three "composition" (like “composition over inheritance”). That isn’t wrong — you just need to be able to distinguish them in an interview.
terms: The tightest relationship — the inner thing is created together with the outer thing and ends together with it.
A looser relationship — the inner thing comes from outside and remains alive even after the outer thing dies.
The loosest — two things just know each other, there is no owner.
The lifespan of something — when it is created and when it ends.
Ownership — who is responsible for creating and destroying something.
o8_3.visualCap: A single question separates all three: "If the outer thing disappears, what will happen to the inner thing?" And the answer also tells where the object will be created — inside with new, or injected from outside.

o9_0.name: Coupling and Cohesion — design thermometer
o9_0.desc: Two terms that indicate whether a design is good or bad. And both can be measured.
o9_0.what:
Coupling = the bond between two things. "If A changes, how much will B break?"

Cohesion = the internal binding of a thing. "Are all the elements of this class for the same purpose?"

Analogy: a wardrobe that contains only clothes and they are neatly arranged — high cohesion. A wardrobe that mixes clothes, dishes, books, and tools — low cohesion.

And if you have to open the neighbor's door to open your wardrobe — tight coupling. If it opens by itself — loose coupling.

Good design mantra: low coupling, high cohesion.
o9_0.why:
These two terms are not just theory — both can be measured:

Ways to measure coupling:
• How many other files does a file import?
• How many files need to be changed when a class changes?
• How many other classes must be created to test a class?

Ways to measure cohesion:
• Does the class name cover all its methods?
• Does each method use most of the class's fields?
• Can you describe the class in one line as "it ___" without using "and"?

How to do it:

The simplest and most honest test: "How many things do I need to create to test this class?"

If testing ParkingLot requires the real database, real payment gateway, and real clock — then coupling is very high.

If you can write new ParkingLot(fakeSpots, fakePricing, fakeClock) and test immediately — coupling is low.

Testability is the thermometer for coupling. Anything that is hard to test is also a bad design — always.
gotchas: Zero coupling is impossible — if nothing is connected to anything else, the system won't work. The goal is "loose" coupling, not "no" coupling.
Don't try to increase cohesion by creating many tiny classes. Fifty classes each with a single method is also bad design.
Don't measure coupling only by import count. An import that depends on an entire interface is more dangerous than five small imports.
terms: How much two things are connected — if one changes, how much the other will break.
How much the elements inside a class are linked — whether they all serve the same purpose.
Less connected — easier to change. This is good.
A class does a single job. This is good.
o9_0.visualCap: Four combinations. The best is the top-right: each class does one job and there is little coupling between them. Testability is the most honest way to measure this.

o9_1.name: Dependency Injection — give things from outside
o9_1.desc: The class should not create its own things. And this makes the test three lines long.
o9_1.what:
If ParkingLot needs spots, pricing, and a clock — should it create them itself or request them from outside?

The answer to Dependency Injection: request them from outside.

constructor(private spots: SpotRepository, private clock: Clock)

That's it. That's the whole concept. The name is big, the thing is small.
o9_1.why:
Three big benefits:

1. The test becomes three lines long. Fake spots, fake clock — and the test runs instantly, without a database or network.

2. One class, different configurations. Different pricing for an airport, different for a mall — the ParkingLot code does not change a single line.

3. Coupling is reduced. ParkingLot no longer knows the name ArraySpotRepo — it only knows the SpotRepository interface.

And that third point becomes Chapter 10’s "D" (Dependency Inversion).

How to do it:

The clock case is the most important, because it is most often forgotten.

Any class that writes new Date() or Date.now() becomes impossible to test — because you cannot advance time. The cure is: make time a thing too.

interface Clock { now(): Date }

In production use SystemClock, in tests use FakeClock that you can advance.

The same applies to randomness (Math.random), the file system, and the network. Inject anything that touches the outside world.
gotchas: Don’t inject everything. Creating small value objects (Money, a wrapper around Date) inside is perfectly fine. Inject only what reaches the outside world or can change.
If eight parameters appear in the constructor — that’s a signal that the class is doing too much. Split the class, don’t look for a DI framework.
DI does not mean a "DI library". In 95% of cases a constructor parameter is enough. A library is needed only when the object graph is very large.
Forgetting to create a FakeClock and using setTimeout in the test — the test becomes slow and flaky.
terms: The thing without which the class cannot work — e.g., ParkingLot needs spots.
Providing things to the class from outside, the class does not create them itself.
The most common DI — things come through the constructor.
A fake thing created for testing that works in place of the real one.

o9_2.name: Immutability and Value Objects — cannot be wrong
o9_2.desc: A Money class that simply cannot be negative. And the trap of readonly.
o9_2.what:
Currently your earnings is a number. And a number has no rules of its own — it can be negative, it can be NaN, and it makes no distinction between rupees and pennies.

This is called primitive obsession: keeping everything as a number/string even though that thing has its own rules.

The remedy: create a small Money class that cannot be wrong.
o9_2.why:
And now combine both ideas — immutable value object:

• Never changes after creation (immutable)
• Its identity is its value, not an id (₹100 and ₹100 are the same)

It has three major benefits: (1) an invalid state cannot be created, (2) if you give it to someone else they cannot corrupt it, (3) testing is trivial.

How to do it:

Now a very important point that many people don’t know:

readonly spots: Spot[] — this does not make the array immutable. It only prevents this.spots = .... this.spots.push(...) still works!

Two real approaches:

1. ReadonlyArray<Spot> — now push will also give an error (compile time).
2. Defensive copy — when exposing, return [...this.#spots] so the outside code can do whatever it wants.
gotchas: readonly array push does not stop — this is the most common TypeScript misconception. Use ReadonlyArray<T>.
Don’t store money as a float. 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3. Always keep money as an integer and divide when displaying.
Don’t turn everything into a value object. Only create one when it has its own rules (Money, PlateNumber, Email) — a plain number is fine for simple counts.
Don’t give a setter in a value object. It defeats the whole point. If you need to change it, return a new object.
terms: An object that never changes after creation. If it needs to change, a new one is created.
A small class whose identity is its VALUE, not its id — e.g., ₹100 and ₹100 are the same.
Keeping everything as a number/string even though that thing has its own rules.
Returning a copy of an internal array/object when exposing it.
o9_2.visualCap: readonly’s trick: it only prevents reassignment, not internal mutation. And the benefit of a value object: an invalid state cannot be created, and testing is a one-line job.

o9_4.name: Shallow and Deep copy — The name of the Chapter 1 mistake
o9_4.desc: There are two ways to make a copy, and one silently changes the original.
o9_4.what:
In Chapter 1 I left out a small point. Remember?

const s = spots[0];
s.takenBy = "anything";
// we only copied a variable... and the original changed

That thing is called: you didn't copy the object, you only copied its reference.

In JavaScript, object variables don't hold the object — they hold its reference (address). So const s = spots[0] means "s also holds the same address". Two names, one object.
o9_4.why:
Now the real danger is here, and it's hidden in [...arr].

You wrote in Chapter 3: get spots() { return [...this.#spots]; } — "I'm giving a copy, it's safe".

That's half true. [...arr] creates a new array, but it contains the same old Spot objects' references. In other words:

✓ If the outside code does copy.push(...) — your array is safe
✗ If the outside code does copy[0].takenBy = "X" — your Spot changed

This is the most sneaky bug, because the code looks like you gave a copy.

How to do it:

Three solutions, each has its place:

1. Deep copy — structuredClone(). Completely new. But it turns classes into plain objects (methods disappear), so it's only suitable for plain data.

2. Your own clone() — class creates its own copy. Most controlled method.

3. Make immutable — best. If Spot cannot change, you don't need a copy. That's why we made Money and PlateNumber immutable.

In other words, the immutability lesson from Chapter 9 is the cleanest cure for this problem — eliminate the need for a copy.
gotchas: [...arr] and {...obj} are both SHALLOW. They only copy one level. This is the most common misunderstanding.
structuredClone() turns classes into plain objects — methods disappear. It's only for plain data.
Don't use JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) for deep copy. It turns Dates into strings, eats undefined and Map/Set, and crashes on circular references.
readonly Spot[] only protects the ARRAY (you can't push), not the inner Spot objects. Type-level readonly and actual immutability are two different things.
terms: The address (reference) of an object, not the object itself. Two variables can hold the same object's address.
A top-level copy — not of the inner objects, only their references are copied.
A full copy — everything inside is newly created.
Create a copy before sending it out, so the receiver cannot modify the original.
o9_4.visualCap: A shallow copy creates a new container but keeps the old references inside. So [...arr] protects the array, but not the inner objects — and this is the most sneaky bug.

o10_0.name: S — Single Responsibility: one class, one responsibility
o10_0.desc: A class should have only one reason to change. And "reason" means "person".
o10_0.what:
Definition: A class should have only one reason to change.

"One reason to change" is often misunderstood. It does not mean "one method". It means: there should be only one person (or team) behind a class's change.

Your ParkingLot currently does all of this: manages spots, calculates fees, sends notifications, generates reports. Now think about who changes them:

• Spots logic → operations team
• Fee logic → finance team
• Notification → marketing team
• Report → management

Four different people, one file. This is the violation of SRP.
o10_0.why:
The practical downside is direct: the finance team asked to change the rate, you opened ParkingLot.ts — and accidentally broke the notification code. The marketing team's feature failed that night.

When things that change for completely different reasons are in one file, each change risks breaking the other.

And this is just another aspect of Chapter 9's cohesion — we now have a better question to measure it: "who changes it?"

How to do it:

Testing approach: write the class's responsibility in one line, without "and".

✗ "ParkingLot manages spots and calculates fees and sends SMS"
✓ "ParkingLot allocates and releases spots"
✓ "PricingPolicy extracts fee from ticket and time"
✓ "Notifier sends a message"

And a warning: Don't take SRP too far. Creating a separate class for every method ("Anemic domain model") is also a bad design. The test is about "who changes it", not about "count of responsibilities".
gotchas: SRP does not mean "one method per class". ParkingLot can have 6 methods, if they are all part of the same responsibility.
If taken too far it becomes an "anemic domain model" — where each class holds only data and all logic lives in separate "Service" classes. That's just procedural code wearing a class mask.
The test is "who changes it". Two methods that always change together should be in the same class — even if they appear unrelated.
terms: A class should have only one reason to change.
The task for which this class is responsible.
The person or team whose direction causes this code to change.
o10_0.visualCap: The real SRP test is not "how many methods there are", but "how many different people change it". Four teams in one file = each change risks breaking another team's feature.

o10_1.name: O and L — Open/Closed and Liskov
o10_1.desc: Both you have already built. Today just the name and scope.
o10_1.what:
O — Open/Closed: "Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification." In other words, it is open for adding new features, but closed for changing existing code.

You implemented this in Chapter 4. Remember that git diff --stat that showed 0 changes when you added WalletPayment? That was live proof of Open/Closed.

L — Liskov Substitution: "Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types." A child can replace its parent without breaking anything.

You have also done this — in Chapter 7 ElectricCar violated it (maxHours changed from 24 to 8), and your contract test caught it.
o10_1.why:
The relationship between them is deep: If Liskov is broken, Open/Closed breaks automatically.

Because if a child cannot replace its parent, you will have to write if (v instanceof ElectricCar) — and that forces you to change the old code.

Therefore the order is: first fix Liskov (correct hierarchy or composition), then Open/Closed resolves itself.

How to do it:

And now covariance and contravariance — the technical forms of Liskov that are asked in interviews.

When overriding, the child:

• Can return a more specific type than the parent (covariance) ✓ — because the caller gets what it expects, and even more.
• Can accept a more general type than the parent (contravariance) ✓ — because whatever the caller provides will still work.

If you do the opposite — return a less specific type, or require a stricter parameter — Liskov will be violated.

Memory aid: "generous in taking, strict in giving." Take as much as you want, but never give less than promised.
gotchas: Open/Closed does not mean "never change old code". Bug fixes and refactoring are perfectly fine. It is about NEW FEATURES.

Don't create an extension point for everything. Having 15 interfaces where 12 have only a single implementation is over-engineering. Create an extension point only when another implementation is truly expected or needed for testing.
TypeScript treats method parameters as bivariant (for backward compatibility) — meaning it also allows unsafe contravariance. Enable strictFunctionTypes: true.
Don't measure Liskov only with type-checking. The compiler checks shape, not behavior. Contract tests are the real verification.
terms: Open for new features, closed for changing existing code.
A child can replace its parent without breaking anything.
A place where new behavior can be added without touching existing code.
The child can return a MORE specific type than the parent — this is safe.
The child can accept a MORE general type than the parent — this is also safe.
o10_1.visualCap: "generous in taking, strict in giving." The child can request a more general type and return a more specific type — both are safe. Doing the opposite breaks Liskov.

o9_3.name: Law of Demeter — don't talk to strangers
o9_3.desc: One dot is fine, three dots are dangerous. And why that train wreck breaks.
o9_3.what:
A small rule with a big impact. A method should only talk to:

1. Itself (this)
2. Its fields
3. Its parameters
4. Objects it created

In other words, talk to your neighbors, not to your neighbors' neighbors.

Analogy: you need to buy something from a shopkeeper. Would you reach into his pocket and take the money yourself? No — you say "give me the item for this price" and he handles it. But in code we often reach into pockets: lot.getSpots()[0].getVehicle().getOwner().getAddress().city
o9_3.why:
A long chain like that is called a train wreck, and it is dangerous because each dot is a dependency.

a.b().c().d() makes you depend on the internal structure of a, b, and c. If any one of them changes — your code breaks.

And it also breaks the encapsulation discussed in Chapter 3: if you can write lot.getSpots()[0].takenBy, then making Spot private is pointless.

How to do it:

The solution is one line: "tell, don't ask" — don't request data and do the work yourself, just tell it what to do.

Wrong: if (lot.getSpots().filter(s => s.isFree()).length > 0) { ... }
Correct: if (lot.hasFreeSpot()) { ... }

And one important exception: this rule does not apply to fluent APIs. arr.filter().map().reduce() or builder.setA().setB().build() are fine, because each call returns the same thing — you are not meeting new strangers.
gotchas: Don't make this a blind rule. Sometimes a short chain is clearer to read. Ask yourself: "Am I assuming the internal structure of something here?"
When applying this, many delegation methods can be created (the boilerplate from Chapter 8). That's fine — but if there are too many, the class division may be wrong.
Fluent APIs (filter/map/builder) are exempt from this rule. There each call returns the same thing.
terms: A rule: only talk to your neighbors, not to their neighbors.
Code like a.b().c().d().e() — looks like a train box, and breaks like one too.
"Don't request data and do the work yourself — just tell it what to do."
