o10_3.name: Five together — and their relationship
o10_3.desc: These are not separate rules. They are five faces of one thing.
o10_3.what:
The five rules are not separate gems. They actually belong to two groups — and both groups are the two concepts from Chapter 9:

Cohesion principle (are things in the right place?):
S — a class, a reason to change
I — an interface, a type of client

Coupling principle (how tightly things are linked?):
O — a new feature can be added without breaking the old one
L — a child can replace its parent
D — not dependent on business implementation
o10_3.why:
And their relationships are:

L broken → O breaks automatically (because you have to write instanceof)
S broken → I often breaks (a large class becomes a large interface)
D broken → testing becomes impossible (real database is required)
I broken → L often breaks (empty methods break promises)

Therefore fixing one often fixes the others automatically — as you saw: applying composition in Chapter 8 fixed both L and O.

How to do it:

For an interview, give a one-line answer for each principle — and include an example from your code. That will set you apart:

S — "One class, one reason to change. I separated pricing and notification from ParkingLot because finance and marketing needed to change them."
O — "Open for new, closed for old. I created a PaymentMethod interface; adding a new wallet payment changed 0 lines in ParkingLot."
L — "Child replaces parent. My ElectricCar extends Car was breaking it, so I switched to composition."
I — "Small interfaces. My Bike had to leave charge() empty, so I extracted Chargeable."
D — "Not dependent on business implementation. ParkingLot depends on SpotRepository, not on PostgresSpotRepo."
gotchas: Don't treat SOLID as a blind checklist. These are guidelines, not laws. Each has its own cost (more files, more interfaces) and in small scripts that cost can outweigh the benefits.
In an interview, don't just give the definition. Provide a code example for each principle — "I saw this break and fixed it this way". That's the real answer.
Trying to follow the five principles 100% can make the code three times larger. Think: which real problem is this principle actually protecting you from here?
terms: Five principles: SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP.
S and I — whether things are in the right place.
O, L and D — how tightly things are coupled.

o11_1.name: Observer and Decorator — two new
o11_1.desc: One notifies "something happened", the other layers a thing over another.
o11_1.what:
Observer: "When something happens, those who care should get notified — and the one that something happened shouldn't know who is listening."

In our parking lot: when a car is parked, the display board updates, analytics records it, and an SMS is sent. ParkingLot should not know about any of these three.

Decorator: "Wrap an object with another object so that new behavior is added — without changing the original object."

In parking: on top of base pricing add weekend surge, then loyalty discount, then GST. Each is a layer.
o11_1.why:
Observer benefit: ParkingLot code never changes even if 10 new listeners are added. This is a direct illustration of the Open/Closed principle.

And you recognize this — addEventListener is exactly that. The button doesn't know who is listening.

Decorator benefit: layers can be added in any order and in any number. Doing this with inheritance leads to the Chapter 7 explosion (SurgeGstPricing, LoyaltySurgeGstPricing...).

How to do it:

Decorator identification: it implements the same interface as the object it wraps. Therefore the outside code doesn't notice whether there is one layer or five.

A small warning for Observer: if a listener throws an error, the remaining listeners will be skipped. Wrap each listener in try/catch.
gotchas: For Observer, forgetting to handle listener errors — if one listener fails, the others are skipped. try/catch is essential.
Forgetting to remove a listener = memory leak. When a component/screen is disposed, be sure to call removeListener.
The order matters for Decorator. Apply GST first or discount first — the result will differ. Pin the order with tests.
Debugging many decorator layers becomes difficult. If there are more than 3-4, consider whether you really need all of them.

The thing on which something happens.
The one that receives the notification.
Add a new object on top of an existing object to introduce new behavior without changing the original.

o11_2.name: Template Method, and the truth about Singleton
o11_2.desc: A framework where empty slots are filled. And a pattern that should often be eliminated.
o11_2.what:
Template Method: the parent writes the entire sequence of work, and leaves some steps abstract for the children to fill.

In parking: "the way a car enters" is always the same — validate, find a spot, allocate, create a ticket, notify. But in each lot the method of finding a spot can differ.

Singleton: "only one object of this class can be created, and it is obtained from a single place throughout the program."
o11_2.why:
Now the truth about Singleton, because it is asked in interviews and most people only show its code:

Singleton is essentially a global variable, hidden inside a class. And it has three major drawbacks:

1. Testing becomes impossible — the state of one test persists into the next test. Test order starts to matter.
2. Hidden dependency — Config.getInstance() is written inside the class, not visible in the constructor. The reader does not realize that this class depends on Config.
3. DIP is broken — you become dependent on a concrete class instead of an interface.

How to handle it:

In most cases the proper remedy for Singleton is DI (Chapter 9): create a single object — in main.ts — and pass it wherever needed.

You get the benefit of “one object”, and all three drawbacks disappear: you can provide a different object in tests, the dependency is visible in the constructor, and you stay dependent on an interface.

Best interview answer: “Singleton controls the count of an object, but it becomes a global state and testability suffers. I usually create one instance and inject it — same benefit, zero drawbacks.”
gotchas: Template method (park()) should be kept final/override-proof — if a child overrides it, the entire sequence will break. Since TypeScript has no final, indicate it with a comment.
Providing many hooks makes the Template Method hard to understand. If there are more than 2-3 hooks, Strategy is better.
Don’t associate Singleton with “thread safety” — JavaScript is single-threaded. The real concerns are testability and hidden dependencies.
Some things truly should be single (database connection pool, logger). Even then, create one instance and inject it — don’t write getInstance().
terms: The parent writes the work framework, and the children fill the empty slots.
The empty slot that a child can fill.
A pattern where only one object of the class can be created.
Something that is single throughout the program and can be accessed from anywhere.

o11_0.name: Strategy and Factory — you have already built this
o11_0.desc: Make behavior an object. And give the object a name.
o11_0.what:
Strategy pattern: "There are many ways to do a task. Make each way an object, and provide the needed one from outside."

You have built this three times:

• PaymentMethod — many ways to receive money (Ch 4)
• PowerSource, ServiceLevel — car features (Ch 8)
• PricingPolicy — many ways to calculate fee (Ch 10)

Factory pattern: "Keep the decision of creating an object in one place, so the caller doesn't have to think about which one to create."

You also built this in Chapter 2: Lot.withFloors("Airport", 5, 100).
o11_0.why:
Now see why a name is important. In a team meeting there are two points:

Without a name: "I am thinking of putting the pricing logic behind an interface and passing it via the constructor so that the weekend version can be different and we can provide a mock in tests..."

With a name: "We make Pricing a Strategy."

That's it. This is the real benefit of patterns — a language for discussion. They don't give a new design; they give a name to your existing design.

How to do it:

A very important warning: do not choose a pattern first.

Wrong approach: "let's apply a Factory pattern here."
Correct approach: "the problem here is... (solution emerges)... oh, its name is Factory."

Choosing a pattern first leads to over-engineering — like having 4 interfaces and an AbstractFactory in a small script. That doesn't solve any problem; it only demonstrates the pattern.
gotchas: Do not pick a pattern first. "Let's apply a Factory here" is a wrong start — first identify the problem, then the solution, then the name.
The switch inside the Factory is fine — it's the single place where external data is turned into objects. Copying that switch everywhere is wrong.
Don't turn a small script into 300 lines by creating four interfaces for a Strategy. Use Strategy only when behavior truly changes.
terms: A well-known solution to a recognized problem, which has an established name.
Encapsulate behavior in an object that can be supplied from outside — so it can be changed.
Separate the object-creation work to a different place, so the caller doesn't have to decide which one to create.
A static method that creates and returns the appropriate object. The most common form.
o11_0.visualCap: Patterns don't give a new design — they name your existing design. And that name makes communication within the team ten times faster.

o11_3.name: Builder and Adapter — the two that are used daily
o11_3.desc: One is the remedy for a long constructor, the other for linking legacy code to your code.
o11_3.what:
Two patterns that appear most often in both machine coding interview and real work.

Builder: when creating an object requires 6-7 pieces, some of which are optional. Writing new ParkingLot("A", 5, 100, 0, true, null, 30) in a constructor becomes a puzzle.

Adapter: when external code (a library, an old SDK) does not match your interface. You cannot change it, so you wrap it.
o11_3.why:
The real reason for Builder is not just "readable". There are two deeper reasons:

1. The object remains incomplete until built, and validation happens once at build(). That means a "half-built object" (Chapter 2) never leaves the code.
2. You don’t have to create six separate constructors for optional parameters (and overloading doesn’t really exist in TypeScript — Chapter 6).

The reason for Adapter is DIP (Chapter 10). Your domain requires PaymentMethod. An external library provides RazorpayClient with a completely different interface. The Adapter stands in the middle and connects the two — and your domain doesn’t even know the library’s name.

How to do it:

Builder has an essential rule: perform validation in build(), not in every setter. Because having an incomplete object in intermediate steps is acceptable — it’s still being constructed. The real check should happen when it leaves the builder.

And for Adapter: place the adapter in infra/, not in domain/. Because it knows the outside world — and the domain should not be aware of external details (DIP, Chapter 10).

A small bonus: Adapter makes testing much easier. Provide a FakePayment instead of the real Razorpay — it works without any network call.
gotchas: Don’t put validation in Builder’s setters. Having an incomplete object in intermediate steps is fine — all validation should be in build(), in one place. Some checks (like "valet needs large spots") can’t be applied in a single setter.
Don’t create a Builder for every class. If there are fewer than three parameters, a normal constructor is better — a Builder has its own cost (an extra whole class).
Putting the Adapter in domain/ breaks DIP, because the domain starts importing the external library. The Adapter should always be in infra/.
Don’t put business logic inside the Adapter. Its only job is translation. If it contains "if amount is greater than 500 then...", that belongs in the domain.

Methods that return themselves so that calls can be chained.
Wrapping something in another interface so it can work with your code.
External code that you didn’t write and cannot modify.
o11_3.visualCap: Builder: the incomplete object stays inside until build() validates it once and returns it. Adapter: wrap the external library in your own interface — the domain never even knows its name.

o10_2.name: I and D — Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion
o10_2.desc: Small interfaces, and don’t let the higher-level depend on the lower-level.
o10_2.what:
I — Interface Segregation: "Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use."

In other words: instead of creating one large interface, create several small ones. Otherwise the class that implements it will have to leave half the methods empty — and an empty method is a lie.

D — Dependency Inversion: "High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions."

You built this in Chapter 9: ParkingLot no longer depends on PostgresSpotRepo, it depends on the SpotRepository interface.
o10_2.why:
"Why the term 'Inversion'? Because normally the arrow points top-to-bottom: ParkingLot → Postgres. In other words, the business logic depends on the database.

With DI the arrow reverses: ParkingLot → SpotRepository ← PostgresSpotRepo. Now both depend on the interface, and that interface stays with the ParkingLot — with the business.

That means: the database is now a servant of the business logic, not its master. Change the database, the business logic won’t change a line. That’s the "inversion".

How to do it:

A quick test for ISP: if a class leaves a method of an interface empty or writes throw new Error("not supported"), the interface is too large.

And for DIP: where should the interface live? The wrong answer many give: "in the database folder". The correct answer: in the business folder — because it serves a business need, not a database offering.
gotchas: Don’t make interfaces so small that each method gets its own interface. Keep together the methods that are always used together.
DIP does not mean "an interface for everything". It applies to things that interact with the outside world (database, network, file, time) or that have multiple implementations.
Putting an interface accidentally in the infra folder — then DIP is only on paper, not in practice, because the domain is still importing infra.
"throw new Error(not supported)" is the clearest sign of an ISP violation. Whenever you feel like writing it, pause and consider breaking the interface.
terms: Several small interfaces are better than one large one.
An interface with so many methods that no one can implement all of them.
The higher-level module should not depend on the lower-level; both should depend on an interface.
High = business rule (parking logic). Low = implementation (Postgres, SMS API).
o10_2.visualCap: In DIP the arrow reverses. The interface stays with the business (it’s a business need), and the database fulfills it. Therefore changing the database does not change a single line of business logic.

o12_1.name: Testing — a mirror of design
o12_1.desc: If a test is hard to write, the design is also bad. Always.
o12_1.what:
The biggest benefit of testing is not catching bugs. It is: testing shows your design back to you.

If writing a test is hard, the reason is always one of these:

• Class creates its own things → DIP broken (Ch 9)
• Class does too much → SRP broken (Ch 10)
• Too much setup required → high coupling
• Test order matters → global state / Singleton (Ch 11)

In other words, pain in writing tests = disease in design. Fix the design instead of fixing the test.
o12_1.why:
There are three types of test doubles that are asked about in interviews:

Stub — just returns a fixed answer. FakeClock that always returns the same time.
Mock — also remembers how it was called. FakeNotifier that keeps a sent[] array.
Fake — a small version of the real thing. ArraySpotRepo used instead of the real PostgresSpotRepo.

Practically: Fake is the best, because it actually works. Overusing mocks makes the test tied to the implementation — refactoring breaks the tests even if behavior stays the same.

How to do it:

And another thing special in OOP: Design by Contract. Every public method has three promises:

Precondition — "what I need" (plate not empty) Postcondition — "what I will give" (ticket or null, and spot will be filled) Invariant — "what will always be true" (earnings never negative)

And these three become directly part of the test. In other words, writing the contract writes the test automatically.
gotchas: Don’t bend the test to fit the design. If writing a test is hard, change the design — the test is telling you something.
Overusing mocks ties the test to the implementation. Test "what happened" instead of "how it was done".
Using new Date() or Math.random() in a test makes it flaky. Inject them (Chapter 9).
Don’t try to test every private method. Test public behavior; if a private method is wrong, some public test will fail.
terms: A test of a small piece in isolation, without database/network.
A fake object that stands in for the real thing.
A fake that only returns a predetermined answer.

Each method has three promises: what it needs (pre), what it returns (post), and what will always be true (invariant).

o12_2.name: OOP vs FP — and when OOP is the wrong choice
o12_2.desc: Two ways of thinking, two kinds of benefits. And honestly: OOP is not right everywhere.
o12_2.what:
People view OOP and FP as "enemies". That's wrong — they are two solutions to the same problem, and each has its own advantage.

OOP: data and the functions that work on it together, and data is hidden.
FP: data simple and open, functions separate, and data never changes — if it needs to change, a new one is created.

And an interesting point: you used both in this book. Money and PlateNumber are immutable value objects — they follow FP thinking, inside OOP.
o12_2.why:
The real difference lies in a choice called the expression problem:

In OOP, adding a new type is easy (create a new class, no existing code changes) but adding a new operation is hard (you have to add a method to every class).

In FP it’s the opposite: adding a new operation is easy (write a new function) but adding a new type is hard (you have to modify the switch in every function).

So the question is: what changes more in your system — types or operations?

In a parking lot, types change more (new vehicles, new payment methods) — therefore OOP is the right choice. In a data-processing pipeline, operations change more — there FP is better.

How to proceed:

And honestly — when OOP is the wrong choice:

1. Small scripts. A 50-line data script — adding 4 interfaces and DI is over-engineering.
2. Data transformation. Read a CSV, filter, sum — map/filter/reduce classes are far better.
3. When there is no state. A pure calculation — wrapping it in a class is pointless.
4. Very high concurrency. Shared mutable state creates race conditions. Immutable data is safe there.

The best answer is often mixed: OOP on the outside (structure, boundaries), FP on the inside (calculations, transformations). As you did — OOP classes that contain immutable Money and pure calculate() methods.
gotchas: Don’t treat OOP vs FP like a religion. Both have their own advantages and they appear together in real code.
Adding interfaces and DI to small scripts is over-engineering. Ask yourself: "Will this code change in six months or will it run once and be done?"
Immutability is not against OOP. Money, PlateNumber, Duration — all are immutable OOP objects, and they are your best design.
If asked in an interview “Is OOP better or FP”, don’t pick one. Explain the expression problem and ask what changes more in the system.
terms: A mindset where data and functions are separate, and data does not change (immutable).
Same input yields same output, and nothing in the world changes.
A choice: whether adding new TYPES should be easy or adding new OPERATIONS.
o12_2.visualCap: Expression problem: In OOP, new types are cheap, new operations expensive. In FP it’s the opposite. The right question is — what changes more in your system?

o13_0.name: Architecture review — look back
o13_0.desc: What was built, what was left out, and what each decision cost.
o13_0.what:
The whole book's journey in one line: from a 60-line procedural file to a layered, tested, extensible system.

And at every turn of that journey there was a decision. A review means writing down those decisions — and their cost as well.

Because every good design has a cost. Composition reduced classes from 24 to 4, but increased the number of objects. DI reduced tests to 3 lines, but introduced the need for a composition root.
o13_0.why:
The difference between junior and senior is this:

Junior says: "I built this."
Senior says: "I chose this, left that, and this will become wrong."

And the strongest answer in an interview is that one. Everyone can answer "What is encapsulation?". "I applied encapsulation in my parking lot because I wrote four attacks myself, and after that those four attacks didn't even compile" — no one else can give that answer.

How to do it:

The review should have four sections:

1. Layers — which layer knows what, and what it doesn't know.
2. Decisions — what was thought, what was chosen, what was left out, why. 3. Metrics — before/after numbers for each chapter in one place. 4. Limits — what is still broken, and if the system grew tenfold, what would break first.

The fourth section impresses the most, because it shows that you don't just love your work, you keep track of it.
gotchas: "What was left out" section should not be skipped. That part shows that you chose deliberately, not just followed a tutorial.
Don't guess numbers. Run grep and wc to write the actual numbers — a single wrong number breaks the credibility of the whole document.
In "What is still broken" don't write "nothing". Every system has issues, and not showing them is the biggest red flag.
terms: Looking at your own design from the outside and documenting its decisions.
The cost of each decision — what you gained versus what you left out.
A portion of code with its own responsibility that only knows about the layer below it.

o13_1.name: Elevator System — now do it alone
o13_1.desc: New domain, no hint. Only requirements and a checklist.
o13_1.what:
Now a new system. And this time no step-by-step.

Requirements:

• In a building there are multiple elevators, and multiple floors
• People can call an elevator from any floor (up or down)
• Inside the elevator people press floor buttons
• The system must decide which elevator will take which request
• Each elevator has its own state: moving (up/down), stopped, door open
• Some elevators can be in service mode (won’t take any request)
• Some elevators stop only at certain floors (e.g., only even floors)
• In an emergency all elevators go to the ground floor and open their doors
o13_1.why:
This is deliberately separate from the parking lot:

In a parking lot things stay (spot occupied or empty). In an elevator things move — the elevator’s state changes every second.

So here a new concept appears that wasn’t in parking: state machine. And the same questions you learned throughout the book will apply.

How to do it:

The way to work — exactly the same as in the book:

1. First write procedural code. Messy, a single file. And refactor it.
2. Extract classes. Write each class’s responsibility in one line.
3. What can change? That becomes an interface. (Which elevator to choose — this is a strategy.)
4. Are there multiple forms of the same thing? That is polymorphism. (Normal elevator, service elevator, even-floor elevator.)
5. What to inject? (Clock — because tests of elevator movement should run without real time.)
6. Write every contract, then write its test.

And a hint I’m giving because it’s new: don’t build a mountain of if-else for the elevator’s state. Think of the state as something that can be an object itself.
gotchas: Don’t try to write a "good design" straight away. First write messy code and refactor — that’s the approach used throughout the book and it works.
Using a string and an if-else chain for state is the most common mistake. In a state machine each state can be a class that returns the next state.
Don’t try to make the elevator selection algorithm perfect. It’s a Strategy — first write a simple one, then add a better one later. That’s the Open/Closed principle.
Don’t leave writing tests until the end. Write a test for each class as you go — otherwise design flaws will remain hidden.
terms: Applying something learned in one place to another — that’s the true measure of learning.
What to build, without specifying how.
The current condition of something — e.g., an elevator "stopped" or "going up".

An entity with a defined set of states that moves from one state to another only along predetermined paths. For example, an elevator: stopped → going up → door open → stopped. An elevator cannot go directly from "going up" to "door open" — it must stop first.

o3_1.name: Getters and setters — let them read, don't let them change
o3_1.desc: You want to show data outside but not let it be changed. And a setter is often the wrong answer.
terms: A method that reads the data and hands it over, but doesn't let it be changed.
A method that changes the data — and can check the rules while changing it.
A value that isn't stored but worked out every time — like "how many spots are free".
o3_1.what:
You made #earnings private — but now whoever builds the report needs it. So what do we do?

Make a getter: a method that reads and hands over the value but doesn't let it be changed.

In TypeScript there are two ways: a normal method (getEarnings()) or the get keyword (get earnings()). The second one you read like a property — lot.earnings — but it is really a method.
o3_1.why:
Now an important point, which many OOP tutorials teach wrongly.

Making a getter and setter for every private field defeats the whole point.

If you made #earnings private and then also made setEarnings(), you saved nothing — anyone can write lot.setEarnings(-99999). You just built a longer road to make the same mistake.

The right question is: "what does the outside need to do with this data?" Needs to build a report? Then give only a getter. Needs to collect a fee? Then give collectFee(amount) — which will check the rules inside.

How to do it:

A good rule:

• Getter — when the outside needs to see the value. Often right.
• Setter — when the outside needs to set the value directly. Often wrong. Give a task-oriented method instead (collectFee, park) that checks the rules inside itself.

And one small but lovely thing: some values shouldn't be stored at all. If you store "how many spots are free" it can go stale. Work it out every time instead. Such a value is called a derived value, and it can never be wrong.
gotchas: Making getter+setter for every field = the whole point of private is gone. This is the most common OOP mistake.
A getter for an array or object hands over the inside thing directly — and the outside can change it. Give a copy ([...arr]) or make it readonly.
get earnings() and #earnings can't have the same name without the #. That's why people write _earnings in TypeScript — but # is better.
Don't do heavy work inside a getter. People think it's a property (cheap), and read it 1000 times in a loop.

o4_0.name: What is abstraction — and how it differs from encapsulation
o4_0.desc: One hides data, the other hides the method. The two go together.
terms: Hiding the inner mess and showing the outside only what is necessary.
The actual code of "how it happens".
A promise — "I can do this job", without saying how.
o4_0.what:
Think you drive a car. You turn the steering and the car turns. You don't need to know whether inside it's rack-and-pinion or hydraulic.

The steering wheel is an abstraction: it tells you what can be done (turning), and hides how it happens.

And the best part: if the company changes the steering's inner mechanism, you don't have to learn to drive again. That is the whole reward of abstraction.

Definition: Abstraction means exposing what an object can do while hiding how it does it.
o4_0.why:
The easiest way to remember the difference:

Encapsulation — "don't touch my safe." (data)
Abstraction — "you don't need to know which company made the safe or how its lock works." (the method)

The two go together. Encapsulation makes abstraction possible: if the data isn't private, your "method" won't stay hidden, because people will touch the data directly and build their own method.

How to do it:

In our parking lot there are right now two places that need abstraction:

1. Payment. ParkingLot should only know: "money can be taken". Cash, UPI, card — that shouldn't be its headache.

2. Vehicle. Every vehicle has its own size and its own rate. ParkingLot should ask "what's your rate", not decide itself with an if-else.

Both need separate tools — and the next two lessons are exactly that.
gotchas: Abstraction doesn't mean "hide everything". Hide more than needed and people will look for workarounds. Hide only what can change.
In an interview you must be able to tell encapsulation and abstraction apart. Remember one line: encapsulation hides data, abstraction hides the method.

o7_0.name: The mountain of subclasses — count it yourself
o7_0.desc: Two different things together need four classes. Three things — eight.
terms: When two or three things combine and multiply the number of classes many times over.
Two things that are completely independent of each other — like "being electric" and "being handicap-accessible".
o7_0.what:
You have Car, Bike, Truck. Now three new things arrive:

• Is it electric or not
• Is it for handicap use or not
• Is it VIP or not

These three are completely independent of each other — an electric vehicle can be handicap and VIP too. Such independent things are called orthogonal.

Now count: 3 vehicle types × 2 (electric or not) × 2 (handicap or not) × 2 (VIP or not) = 24 classes.
o7_0.why:
And this isn't just a counting problem. Every new thing doubles the classes:

Add one more thing (like "is it diesel") → 48 classes.
One more → 96.

And most of these classes will have the same code copied. ElectricCar and ElectricTruck will both have the same plugIn() code written — because their parents are different and they can't share that code.

This is inheritance's biggest limit: it works in only one dimension.

How to do it:

The root of it is this: a class has only one parent (the rule from Chapter 5). So if you need two independent things together, the hierarchy has no room for them — you'll have to make a new class for every combination.

And when you build this mountain yourself and count it, you'll realise on your own what the answer should be: instead of making these things "classes", make them "things" that can be kept inside the vehicle.

But don't think about the answer yet. Today just build the mountain and count it.
gotchas: Really write this code, don't just read it. After writing eight classes the tiredness itself will tell you something is wrong — and that is the lesson of this chapter.
Don't think "I won't make so many classes". These classes get made one by one, over months, and each one feels right at the time.
In real codebases this mountain stands up by itself in 3 years. Nobody sits down one day and makes 24 classes.

o12_0.name: Anti-patterns — the ones that got names
o12_0.desc: God object, anemic model, and the mistakes you made yourself.
terms: A solution that looks fine at first but becomes a problem later.
One class that knows everything and does everything.
Classes that hold only data and no behaviour — procedural code in the mask of classes.
A method that uses another class's data more than its own class's.
Keeping everything as a number/string, even though it has its own rules.
o12_0.what:
An anti-pattern means a solution that looks fine at first and becomes a burden later. The five most common:

1. God object — one class that does everything. Your ParkingLot from Chapter 9 was on this road: park, unpark, fee, SMS, report, CSV.

2. Anemic domain model — classes with only data, all the logic in separate "Service" classes. This comes from taking SRP too far.

3. Feature envy — a method that plays with other people's data more than its own.

4. Primitive obsession — the state before the Money in Chapter 9.

5. Shotgun surgery — one small change, five files (the if-else from Chapter 6).
o12_0.why:
Pause a bit on the anemic domain model, because it is the most hidden one.

Many codebases look like this: class Ticket { id; plate; enteredAt; } — only data. And then class TicketService { calculateHours(t); isExpired(t); } — all the logic.

It works. But it is procedural code, just wearing a mask of classes. Data in one place, the functions that work on it in another — exactly the problem from Chapter 1, and the same harm: any Service can change Ticket's data.

And an honest point: in big systems this is sometimes chosen on purpose (when data comes from a DB and logic lives in separate layers). So don't blindly call it "bad" — just know what you are choosing.

How to do it:

Three measures to spot a god object:

1. The file is 300+ lines
2. The class has 10+ public methods
3. A one-line job can't be written without 2+ "and"s

And the test for feature envy: if a method touches some other object more than this, that method is in the wrong class. Pick it up and move it to where its data is.
gotchas: Don't blindly call an anemic domain model "bad". In big systems it is sometimes chosen on purpose (when data comes from a DB and validation is in a separate layer). Just know what you are choosing.
A god object isn't made in a day. Every method feels right at the time. So keep running the "and" test every 2-3 months.
The refactor for feature envy is the cheapest and has the biggest effect — pick the method up and put it in the class whose data it is using.
